items.stem: Which of the following best describes "inquiry question"?
options: A first-hand experience of a political issue, such as interviewing stakeholders, volunteering with an organisation, observing meetings or taking part in a campaign, which forms the basis of the engagement project
The agreement of a participant to take part in research after being told its purpose, how information will be used and that they can withdraw at any time
Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations
A focused, open question that guides the engagement project and allows analysis of a political issue, often framed with command terms such as “to what extent” or “how”
items.answer: A focused, open question that guides the engagement project and allows analysis of a political issue, often framed with command terms such as “to what extent” or “how”
items.markingKey: D. "inquiry question" is a focused, open question that guides the engagement project and allows analysis of a political issue, often framed with command terms such as “to what extent” or “how”.

items.stem: Briefly explain why linking the issue to key concepts should begin at the planning stage.
items.answer: Choosing activities with concepts such as power, legitimacy or rights in mind ensures that the evidence gathered will support analysis, not just description.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Choosing activities with concepts such as power, legitimacy or rights in mind ensures that the evidence gathered will support analysis, not just description. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a topic and a political issue.
items.answer: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers).
items.markingKey: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source B
Illustrative student proposal: “I am interested in global poverty. I will read reports by the World Bank and Oxfam and write about why poverty exists in the world.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement project proposal)

Outline three points made in Source B about choosing and planning an engagement project. [3]
items.answer: the student is interested in global poverty; they plan to read reports by the World Bank and Oxfam; they plan to write about why poverty exists in the world
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: the student is interested in global poverty; they plan to read reports by the World Bank and Oxfam; they plan to write about why poverty exists in the world. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source D
Illustrative student proposal: “My issue is whether our town should allow a new lithium mine. I will interview a representative of the mining company, members of a local farmers’ cooperative and a regional environmental officer, and attend the public consultation in March.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement project proposal)

Using evidence from Source D, explain why the planned engagement is likely to support effective analysis. [3]
items.answer: It involves several stakeholders with conflicting interests (company, farmers, regulator) and a formal decision-making process, so the student can analyse power, legitimacy and sustainability from multiple perspectives.
items.markingKey: It involves several stakeholders with conflicting interests (company, farmers, regulator) and a formal decision-making process, so the student can analyse power, legitimacy and sustainability from multiple perspectives. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: A student wants to study “China’s rise”. Suggest how they could turn this into a manageable political issue for an engagement project and one engagement activity. [4]
items.answer: Narrow to a specific, accessible issue such as the effect of a Chinese-funded infrastructure project on the student’s region or the debate over a local Confucius Institute; engage by interviewing local officials, business owners or university staff. Award marks for a focused issue (1), link to power or interdependence (1), a feasible first-hand activity (1) and an ethical consideration (1).
items.markingKey: Narrow to a specific, accessible issue such as the effect of a Chinese-funded infrastructure project on the student’s region or the debate over a local Confucius Institute; engage by interviewing local officials, business owners or university staff. Award marks for a focused issue (1), link to power or interdependence (1), a feasible first-hand activity (1) and an ethical consideration (1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Local political issues are more suitable for the engagement project than global ones."
items.answer: Local issues are usually more suitable because they allow genuine engagement, provided their links to wider global politics are analysed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allow first-hand engagement; specific, manageable stakeholders; local issues often reflect global dynamics. Arguments against: global issues (climate, migration) are highly significant; online engagement with global organisations is possible; local focus may limit conceptual range. Supported judgement: Local issues are usually more suitable because they allow genuine engagement, provided their links to wider global politics are analysed.

items.stem: Discuss the view that direct engagement with a political issue produces better understanding than academic research alone. [15]
items.answer: Direct engagement deepens understanding most when it is combined with academic research and theory.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: first-hand evidence and stakeholder perspectives; limits of small samples; value of theory and secondary data; combining both. Possible judgement: Direct engagement deepens understanding most when it is combined with academic research and theory. Markbands (15): 13–15 – sharply focused on the demands of the question; detailed, accurate knowledge of relevant concepts, theories and specific contemporary examples; well-developed, balanced counter-claims; a clear, consistent and well-supported conclusion. 10–12 – focused and well structured; relevant, accurate knowledge and examples; counter-claims addressed; reasoned conclusion. 7–9 – mostly focused; relevant knowledge with some examples; some counter-claims; conclusion stated. 4–6 – some understanding of the demands; limited or general knowledge, mainly descriptive; little evaluation. 1–3 – little understanding; minimal relevant knowledge; no evaluation. 0 – does not reach the standard of band 1.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a student should seek a range of perspectives on their political issue.
items.answer: Political issues involve competing interests; engaging with several stakeholders (officials, activists, affected residents) avoids one-sided conclusions and supports balanced evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Political issues involve competing interests; engaging with several stakeholders (officials, activists, affected residents) avoids one-sided conclusions and supports balanced evaluation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using a student interviewing hawker-centre workers about wages in Singapore as an example, explain equality and the role of the state.
items.answer: The student interviewed four workers and a union representative about the Progressive Wage Model and the cost of living. The engagement links individual experiences of low pay to state policy and debates about equality of outcome.
items.markingKey: Context (The student interviewed four workers and a union representative about the Progressive Wage Model and the cost of living.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The engagement links individual experiences of low pay to state policy and debates about equality of outcome. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to equality and the role of the state.

items.stem: Which method is an example of triangulation?
items.answer: Comparing an official’s interview with council minutes and a campaigner’s account
items.markingKey: Comparing an official’s interview with council minutes and a campaigner’s account. Triangulation compares different sources or methods to test findings.

items.stem: A student claims: "Interviewees with official positions always provide the most reliable evidence." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Officials may defend their institution’s position; their evidence should be weighed and triangulated like any other.
items.markingKey: Officials may defend their institution’s position; their evidence should be weighed and triangulated like any other. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a theoretical perspective and a stakeholder’s perspective.
items.answer: A stakeholder’s perspective is the view of an actual participant based on their interests; a theoretical perspective is an academic framework used to interpret the issue as a whole.
items.markingKey: A stakeholder’s perspective is the view of an actual participant based on their interests; a theoretical perspective is an academic framework used to interpret the issue as a whole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source C
Illustrative student analysis: “The councillor said the council supports refugees, but the housing officer told me that no new funding has been provided. This suggests the council wants to appear legitimate to residents who support refugees while avoiding costs that might be unpopular with others.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report draft)

Outline three points made in Source C about analysing the engagement through concepts, theories and perspectives. [3]
items.answer: the councillor said the council supports refugees; the housing officer said no new funding has been provided; the student infers the council seeks legitimacy while avoiding unpopular costs
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: the councillor said the council supports refugees; the housing officer said no new funding has been provided; the student infers the council seeks legitimacy while avoiding unpopular costs. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: With reference to engagement with a youth climate group in Jakarta, explain how it illustrates the power of non-state actors.
items.answer: A student joined a youth climate group’s campaign on air pollution, interviewed an organiser and a city official, and analysed the city’s air quality data. Comparing the organiser’s and the official’s views shows how youth groups use public pressure and litigation (the 2021 Jakarta air pollution ruling) to influence state policy.
items.markingKey: Context (A student joined a youth climate group’s campaign on air pollution, interviewed an organiser and a city official, and analysed the city’s air quality data.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Comparing the organiser’s and the official’s views shows how youth groups use public pressure and litigation (the 2021 Jakarta air pollution ruling) to influence state policy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the power of non-state actors.

items.stem: A student’s engagement involved a local campaign against the closure of a rural clinic. Identify the levels of analysis that could be connected and explain one link. [4]
items.answer: Levels: local (clinic, residents), national (health budget, austerity), possibly global (IMF programmes, global health workforce migration). Link: national budget cuts driven by fiscal pressures lead to local closures, showing how decisions at one level shape experiences at another. 1 mark per level (max 2) and 2 marks for an explained link.
items.markingKey: Levels: local (clinic, residents), national (health budget, austerity), possibly global (IMF programmes, global health workforce migration). Link: national budget cuts driven by fiscal pressures lead to local closures, showing how decisions at one level shape experiences at another. 1 mark per level (max 2) and 2 marks for an explained link.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The most important skill in the engagement project is the evaluation of evidence."
items.answer: Evaluating evidence is central, but it depends on good engagement and conceptual analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stakeholders have interests; small samples need caution; triangulation underpins credible conclusions. Arguments against: conceptual analysis is equally important; the quality of engagement determines the evidence available; clear communication matters. Supported judgement: Evaluating evidence is central, but it depends on good engagement and conceptual analysis.

items.stem:
Source B
Illustrative student draft: “I went to the climate protest. There were about 300 people. I talked to some of them. They were angry about the government. Then I went home and read about the Paris Agreement.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report draft)

Using evidence from Source B, explain why the draft is descriptive rather than analytical, and how the student could develop it. [4]
items.answer: It only recounts events, gives no specific stakeholder perspectives and makes no link to concepts or theory. The student could develop it by recording specific claims from named or anonymised stakeholders, comparing them with government positions, and explaining the findings through concepts such as legitimacy, sustainability or the power of non-state actors.
items.markingKey: It only recounts events, gives no specific stakeholder perspectives and makes no link to concepts or theory. The student could develop it by recording specific claims from named or anonymised stakeholders, comparing them with government positions, and explaining the findings through concepts such as legitimacy, sustainability or the power of non-state actors. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why applying a theory can help interpret engagement findings.
items.answer: Theories offer explanations of actors’ motives and structures – realism for self-interest, liberalism for cooperation, Marxism for economic power – so findings can be interpreted, compared and challenged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Theories offer explanations of actors’ motives and structures – realism for self-interest, liberalism for cooperation, Marxism for economic power – so findings can be interpreted, compared and challenged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In a Paper 3-style answer, what is the best use of a second case study?
items.answer: To compare with the stimulus and test whether the same concept or explanation applies elsewhere
items.markingKey: To compare with the stimulus and test whether the same concept or explanation applies elsewhere. Comparison shows understanding beyond a single case.

items.stem: Explain the difference between explain and evaluate.
items.answer: “Explain” requires a detailed account of reasons or causes; “evaluate” requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: “Explain” requires a detailed account of reasons or causes; “evaluate” requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Rafael writes: "A case study must be from the same country as the stimulus." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Case studies can come from anywhere; the best are relevant to the concept and allow meaningful comparison.
items.markingKey: Case studies can come from anywhere; the best are relevant to the concept and allow meaningful comparison. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A
Stimulus: Between 2021 and 2023, COVAX delivered nearly 2 billion vaccine doses to 146 economies. Yet by mid-2022, only about one in five people in low-income countries had received a dose, compared with three in four in high-income countries.
— Summary based on Gavi and WHO data (2022–23)

With reference to Source A, explain how the stimulus illustrates inequality in global health governance. [3]
items.answer: Despite a global mechanism, access remained highly unequal, showing that wealthier states’ purchasing power shaped outcomes more than multilateral distribution.
items.markingKey: Despite a global mechanism, access remained highly unequal, showing that wealthier states’ purchasing power shaped outcomes more than multilateral distribution. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source A
Stimulus: In 2023 Australia and Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty. Up to 280 Tuvaluans a year may move to Australia with rights to live, work and study. Australia also committed to help Tuvalu respond to natural disasters and to come to its assistance in the event of military aggression.
— Summary based on the Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (2023)

Outline three points made in Source A about responding to stimulus on a global political challenge using case studies. [3]
items.answer: up to 280 Tuvaluans a year may move to Australia; they gain rights to live, work and study; Australia will assist with disasters and in case of military aggression
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: up to 280 Tuvaluans a year may move to Australia; they gain rights to live, work and study; Australia will assist with disasters and in case of military aggression. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Using Rwanda’s gender quota and Norway’s board quota as an example, explain equality and affirmative measures.
items.answer: Rwanda reserved parliamentary seats for women in 2003; Norway required 40 per cent women on public company boards from 2008. The cases contrast political and economic quotas in very different contexts, allowing evaluation of whether quotas change power.
items.markingKey: Context (Rwanda reserved parliamentary seats for women in 2003; Norway required 40 per cent women on public company boards from 2008.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The cases contrast political and economic quotas in very different contexts, allowing evaluation of whether quotas change power. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to equality and affirmative measures.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The HL global political challenges are best understood as interconnected rather than separate issues."
items.answer: The challenges are deeply interconnected, though each requires precise analysis of its own actors and concepts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate change affects borders, security and health; technology shapes identity and equality; poverty links to health and conflict. Arguments against: separate analysis gives clarity; each challenge has distinct actors and institutions; over-linking can become vague. Supported judgement: The challenges are deeply interconnected, though each requires precise analysis of its own actors and concepts.

items.stem: Examine the view that A single detailed case study is more valuable than several brief examples in answering a stimulus question. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Depth is essential, but the strongest answers combine detailed cases with explicit comparison.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: depth allows analysis of actors and causes; specific evidence; avoids superficial lists. Arguments against: comparison needs at least two cases; range shows breadth of understanding; one case may be unrepresentative. Possible judgement: Depth is essential, but the strongest answers combine detailed cases with explicit comparison. Markbands (15): 13–15 – sharply focused on the demands of the question; detailed, accurate knowledge of relevant concepts, theories and specific contemporary examples; well-developed, balanced counter-claims; a clear, consistent and well-supported conclusion. 10–12 – focused and well structured; relevant, accurate knowledge and examples; counter-claims addressed; reasoned conclusion. 7–9 – mostly focused; relevant knowledge with some examples; some counter-claims; conclusion stated. 4–6 – some understanding of the demands; limited or general knowledge, mainly descriptive; little evaluation. 1–3 – little understanding; minimal relevant knowledge; no evaluation. 0 – does not reach the standard of band 1.

items.stem: Explain why HL global political challenges are interconnected.
items.answer: Issues overlap: climate change affects borders, security and health; technology shapes identity and equality; so a case study may illuminate several challenges at once.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Issues overlap: climate change affects borders, security and health; technology shapes identity and equality; so a case study may illuminate several challenges at once. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The maximum length of the engagement project report (2,000 words); material beyond the limit is not assessed"?
options: word limit
theoretical lens
conclusion
referencing
items.answer: word limit
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of word limit.

items.stem: Distinguish between an evaluative conclusion and a summary conclusion.
items.answer: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations.
items.markingKey: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why careful selection of evidence is necessary in a 2,000-word report.
items.answer: The word limit means that only the most relevant evidence can be included; selecting key quotations and data allows space for analysis and evaluation. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The word limit means that only the most relevant evidence can be included; selecting key quotations and data allows space for analysis and evaluation. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source B
Illustrative conclusion: “The evidence suggests that the youth council had limited influence on the city’s climate policy. Officials welcomed its proposals, but none was adopted in the 2024 budget. However, my evidence comes mainly from two officials and three council members, so stronger evidence from budget documents would test this conclusion further.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report conclusion)

Outline three points made in Source B about writing and reflecting on the engagement project report. [3]
items.answer: the youth council had limited influence on the city’s climate policy; officials welcomed its proposals but none was adopted in the 2024 budget; the evidence comes mainly from two officials and three council members, so budget documents would test it further
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: the youth council had limited influence on the city’s climate policy; officials welcomed its proposals but none was adopted in the 2024 budget; the evidence comes mainly from two officials and three council members, so budget documents would test it further. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Rewrite this descriptive sentence as an analytical one: “I interviewed a police officer and a protester.” [2]
items.answer: E.g. “The police officer framed the protest as a threat to public order, while the protester saw it as a legitimate exercise of rights, revealing a conflict between state authority and liberty.” 1 mark for comparison of perspectives, 1 mark for a link to a concept.
items.markingKey: E.g. “The police officer framed the protest as a threat to public order, while the protester saw it as a legitimate exercise of rights, revealing a conflict between state authority and liberty.” 1 mark for comparison of perspectives, 1 mark for a link to a concept.

items.stem: "Reflection is the most important part of the engagement project report." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Reflection is essential, but it strengthens rather than replaces analysis and evidence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: shows critical awareness; qualifies conclusions; demonstrates learning from engagement. Arguments against: analysis using concepts is central; evidence quality matters more; reflection without analysis is weak. Possible judgement: Reflection is essential, but it strengthens rather than replaces analysis and evidence. Markbands (15): 13–15 – sharply focused on the demands of the question; detailed, accurate knowledge of relevant concepts, theories and specific contemporary examples; well-developed, balanced counter-claims; a clear, consistent and well-supported conclusion. 10–12 – focused and well structured; relevant, accurate knowledge and examples; counter-claims addressed; reasoned conclusion. 7–9 – mostly focused; relevant knowledge with some examples; some counter-claims; conclusion stated. 4–6 – some understanding of the demands; limited or general knowledge, mainly descriptive; little evaluation. 1–3 – little understanding; minimal relevant knowledge; no evaluation. 0 – does not reach the standard of band 1.

items.stem: Define the term "word limit".
items.answer: The maximum length of the engagement project report (2,000 words); material beyond the limit is not assessed
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the maximum length of the engagement project report (2,000 words); material beyond the limit is not assessed. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "informed consent".
items.answer: The agreement of a participant to take part in research after being told its purpose, how information will be used and that they can withdraw at any time
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the agreement of a participant to take part in research after being told its purpose, how information will be used and that they can withdraw at any time. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "triangulation"?
options: Checking findings by comparing evidence from different sources or methods, such as interviews, documents and observation
A matter of public contention that involves power, competing interests or values and decisions about who gets what, and that can be studied at local, national or global levels
The agreement of a participant to take part in research after being told its purpose, how information will be used and that they can withdraw at any time
Acknowledging all sources used, through in-text citations and a reference list in a consistent style, as required by IB academic integrity policy
items.answer: Checking findings by comparing evidence from different sources or methods, such as interviews, documents and observation
items.markingKey: A. "triangulation" is checking findings by comparing evidence from different sources or methods, such as interviews, documents and observation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evaluate (command term)"?
options: The viewpoint of a particular actor or group on a political issue, shaped by their interests, values, identity and position
The final section of the report, which answers the inquiry question with a judgement supported by the evidence and analysis
Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations
The different scales at which a political issue can be examined – individual, local, national, regional and global – and the connections between them
items.answer: Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations
items.markingKey: C. "evaluate (command term)" is make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Including more activities always improves the report." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Quality and depth of analysis matter more than the number of activities; too many reduce space for analysis within 2,000 words.
items.markingKey: Quality and depth of analysis matter more than the number of activities; too many reduce space for analysis within 2,000 words. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Taking part in a simulation alone is always sufficient engagement." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Simulations such as Model UN can be useful, but engagement with real stakeholders and the actual issue usually provides stronger evidence.
items.markingKey: Simulations such as Model UN can be useful, but engagement with real stakeholders and the actual issue usually provides stronger evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Interviewees with official positions always provide the most reliable evidence." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Officials may defend their institution’s position; their evidence should be weighed and triangulated like any other.
items.markingKey: Officials may defend their institution’s position; their evidence should be weighed and triangulated like any other. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between evaluate and explain.
items.answer: “Explain” requires a detailed account of reasons or causes; “evaluate” requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: “Explain” requires a detailed account of reasons or causes; “evaluate” requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why referencing matters in the engagement project.
items.answer: It acknowledges others’ work, allows the reader to check evidence and upholds academic integrity; failure to reference can be treated as academic misconduct.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It acknowledges others’ work, allows the reader to check evidence and upholds academic integrity; failure to reference can be treated as academic misconduct. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a topic and a political issue.
items.answer: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers).
items.markingKey: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to engagement with a food bank in Toronto, explain how it illustrates structural violence and the limits of charity.
items.answer: A student volunteered for six weeks, interviewed the coordinator and two clients, and compared their accounts with municipal data on rising rents. The engagement shows how housing costs and low wages – structural factors – create need that charity alone cannot address, linking local experience to Galtung’s concept.
items.markingKey: Context (A student volunteered for six weeks, interviewed the coordinator and two clients, and compared their accounts with municipal data on rising rents.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The engagement shows how housing costs and low wages – structural factors – create need that charity alone cannot address, linking local experience to Galtung’s concept. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structural violence and the limits of charity.

items.stem: Suggest two contrasting case studies you could use for the identity challenge and explain why they make a good pair. [4]
items.answer: E.g. Catalonia (sub-state nationalism in a democracy) and the Rohingya (exclusion from citizenship in an authoritarian context): they differ in regime type, scale of exclusion and outcomes, allowing comparison of recognition and sovereignty. 1 mark per case (2), 2 marks for the justification.
items.markingKey: E.g. Catalonia (sub-state nationalism in a democracy) and the Rohingya (exclusion from citizenship in an authoritarian context): they differ in regime type, scale of exclusion and outcomes, allowing comparison of recognition and sovereignty. 1 mark per case (2), 2 marks for the justification.

items.stem: Using a report on a school recycling campaign in Accra as an example, explain balancing description and analysis.
items.answer: The draft spent 1,200 words describing meetings and only 300 words on analysis, and concluded “the campaign was interesting”. The report needs to reduce description, analyse stakeholders’ positions using concepts such as sustainability and power, and reach a judgement on the inquiry question.
items.markingKey: Context (The draft spent 1,200 words describing meetings and only 300 words on analysis, and concluded “the campaign was interesting”.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The report needs to reduce description, analyse stakeholders’ positions using concepts such as sustainability and power, and reach a judgement on the inquiry question. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to balancing description and analysis.

items.stem: With reference to a student attending council meetings on a low-emission zone in Lyon, explain how it illustrates legitimacy and sustainability at the local level.
items.answer: The student observed two council debates, interviewed a small-business owner and a cycling campaigner, and surveyed classmates’ families. Different stakeholders’ views show how policy legitimacy depends on balancing environmental goals with economic fairness.
items.markingKey: Context (The student observed two council debates, interviewed a small-business owner and a cycling campaigner, and surveyed classmates’ families.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Different stakeholders’ views show how policy legitimacy depends on balancing environmental goals with economic fairness. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to legitimacy and sustainability at the local level.

items.stem:
Source D
Illustrative conclusion: “The evidence suggests that the youth council had limited influence on the city’s climate policy. Officials welcomed its proposals, but none was adopted in the 2024 budget. However, my evidence comes mainly from two officials and three council members, so stronger evidence from budget documents would test this conclusion further.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report conclusion)

Using evidence from Source D, explain why the conclusion is likely to be credited as evaluative. [4]
items.answer: It reaches a clear judgement (limited influence), supports it with evidence (no proposals adopted) and reflects on the limits of the sample, suggesting how the conclusion could be tested.
items.markingKey: It reaches a clear judgement (limited influence), supports it with evidence (no proposals adopted) and reflects on the limits of the sample, suggesting how the conclusion could be tested. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Local political issues are more suitable for the engagement project than global ones."
items.answer: Local issues are usually more suitable because they allow genuine engagement, provided their links to wider global politics are analysed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allow first-hand engagement; specific, manageable stakeholders; local issues often reflect global dynamics. Arguments against: global issues (climate, migration) are highly significant; online engagement with global organisations is possible; local focus may limit conceptual range. Supported judgement: Local issues are usually more suitable because they allow genuine engagement, provided their links to wider global politics are analysed.

items.stem: "The most important skill in the engagement project is the evaluation of evidence." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Evaluating evidence is central, but it depends on good engagement and conceptual analysis.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: stakeholders have interests; small samples need caution; triangulation underpins credible conclusions. Arguments against: conceptual analysis is equally important; the quality of engagement determines the evidence available; clear communication matters. Possible judgement: Evaluating evidence is central, but it depends on good engagement and conceptual analysis. items.stem: With reference to two case studies, discuss the extent to which states remain the most important actors in addressing global political challenges. [15]
items.answer: States remain central, but non-state and multilateral actors are increasingly important in shaping responses.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: states in border and security policy; NGOs, firms and IGOs in health and technology; COVAX and the Falepili Union; non-state actors depend on states. Possible judgement: States remain central, but non-state and multilateral actors are increasingly important in shaping responses. items.stem: "Reflection is the most important part of the engagement project report." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Reflection is essential, but it strengthens rather than replaces analysis and evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows critical awareness; qualifies conclusions; demonstrates learning from engagement. Arguments against: analysis using concepts is central; evidence quality matters more; reflection without analysis is weak. Supported judgement: Reflection is essential, but it strengthens rather than replaces analysis and evidence. items.stem: Which inquiry question is best framed for an engagement project?
options: What is the youth council?
When was the youth council founded?
Is climate change bad?
To what extent has the city’s youth council influenced local climate policy?
items.answer: To what extent has the city’s youth council influenced local climate policy?
items.markingKey: D. It is focused, open and requires analysis and evaluation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Checking findings by comparing evidence from different sources or methods, such as interviews, documents and observation"?
options: analyse (command term)
triangulation
reflection
informed consent
items.answer: triangulation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of triangulation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "case study".
items.answer: A detailed, specific example of a political issue (a place, event, actor or policy) studied in depth and used as evidence in an answer
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a detailed, specific example of a political issue (a place, event, actor or policy) studied in depth and used as evidence in an answer. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an evaluative conclusion and a summary conclusion.
items.answer: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations.
items.markingKey: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Noah writes: "The engagement project is mainly a literature review." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is centred on the student’s own engagement with a political issue, supported – not replaced – by secondary research.
items.markingKey: It is centred on the student’s own engagement with a political issue, supported – not replaced – by secondary research. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why connecting local engagement to global politics adds depth to the analysis.
items.answer: Local issues often reflect wider dynamics – global markets, international norms or migration flows – so linking levels shows interdependence and the significance of the case.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Local issues often reflect wider dynamics – global markets, international norms or migration flows – so linking levels shows interdependence and the significance of the case. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In a stimulus-based answer, using only the stimulus is enough for full marks." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Higher-mark questions require the candidate to bring in their own specific case studies and knowledge as well as the stimulus.
items.markingKey: Higher-mark questions require the candidate to bring in their own specific case studies and knowledge as well as the stimulus. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a summary conclusion and an evaluative conclusion.
items.answer: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations.
items.markingKey: A summary conclusion repeats what was done; an evaluative conclusion answers the inquiry question with a reasoned judgement, weighs evidence and acknowledges limitations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a political issue and a topic.
items.answer: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers).
items.markingKey: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. migration); a political issue is a specific, contested question about power and decisions within it (e.g. whether a municipality should accept more asylum seekers). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source D
Illustrative student analysis: “The councillor said the council supports refugees, but the housing officer told me that no new funding has been provided. This suggests the council wants to appear legitimate to residents who support refugees while avoiding costs that might be unpopular with others.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report draft)

With reference to Source D, explain how the extract shows analysis rather than description. [3]
items.answer: It compares two stakeholders’ statements, identifies a contradiction and explains it through the concept of legitimacy and competing political pressures, moving beyond reporting what was said.
items.markingKey: It compares two stakeholders’ statements, identifies a contradiction and explains it through the concept of legitimacy and competing political pressures, moving beyond reporting what was said. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source C
Stimulus: In 2023 Australia and Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty. Up to 280 Tuvaluans a year may move to Australia with rights to live, work and study. Australia also committed to help Tuvalu respond to natural disasters and to come to its assistance in the event of military aggression.
— Summary based on the Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (2023)

Using evidence from Source C, explain how the stimulus illustrates the interconnection between the environment and borders challenges. [4]
items.answer: Climate threats to Tuvalu’s territory create a need for new migration pathways across borders, and the treaty combines mobility with security commitments, showing how environmental change reshapes border policy and sovereignty.
items.markingKey: Climate threats to Tuvalu’s territory create a need for new migration pathways across borders, and the treaty combines mobility with security commitments, showing how environmental change reshapes border policy and sovereignty. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: A student’s 2,000-word draft contains 600 words of background on the history of the European Union before reaching their engagement with a local farmers’ protest. Advise the student on how to revise the report. [4]
items.answer: Cut background to a brief context (e.g. under 150 words) linked to the inquiry question; move the focus to the engagement and analysis of stakeholders’ perspectives; use the saved words for evaluation and reflection; ensure all sources are referenced. 1 mark per developed piece of advice.
items.markingKey: Cut background to a brief context (e.g. under 150 words) linked to the inquiry question; move the focus to the engagement and analysis of stakeholders’ perspectives; use the saved words for evaluation and reflection; ensure all sources are referenced. 1 mark per developed piece of advice.

items.answer: It is centred on the student’s own engagement with a political issue, supported – not replaced – by secondary research.

— Constructed practice extract (engagement report draft)

Identify three pieces of evidence or claims in Source B. [3]
items.answer: the councillor said the council supports refugees; the housing officer said no new funding has been provided; the student infers the council seeks legitimacy while avoiding unpopular costs
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: the councillor said the council supports refugees; the housing officer said no new funding has been provided; the student infers the council seeks legitimacy while avoiding unpopular costs. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Using Kenya’s M-Pesa and India’s Aadhaar as an example, explain technology and development.
items.answer: M-Pesa is a private mobile money system; Aadhaar is a state-run biometric identity system linked to welfare and payments. Comparing private and state-led digital systems shows different relationships between technology, power and inclusion.
items.markingKey: Context (M-Pesa is a private mobile money system; Aadhaar is a state-run biometric identity system linked to welfare and payments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Comparing private and state-led digital systems shows different relationships between technology, power and inclusion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to technology and development.

items.stem:
Source D
Illustrative conclusion: “In conclusion, I learned a lot about climate change and the youth council. It was a great experience and I met many interesting people. Climate change is a very important issue for everyone.”
— Constructed practice extract (engagement report conclusion)

Using evidence from Source D, explain why the conclusion is weak and how the student could improve it. [4]
items.answer: It does not answer the inquiry question, gives no evidence and is personal rather than analytical. The student should state a judgement on the inquiry question, support it with key evidence from the engagement, link it to concepts and reflect on the limitations of the evidence.
items.markingKey: It does not answer the inquiry question, gives no evidence and is personal rather than analytical. The student should state a judgement on the inquiry question, support it with key evidence from the engagement, link it to concepts and reflect on the limitations of the evidence. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Personal engagement makes political analysis less objective."
items.answer: Engagement introduces risks of bias, but structured reflection and multiple perspectives make it a strength rather than a weakness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: students may adopt the views of those they meet; limited sample of stakeholders; emotional involvement. Arguments against: first-hand evidence reveals realities hidden in secondary sources; reflection and multiple perspectives reduce bias; all analysis involves perspective. Supported judgement: Engagement introduces risks of bias, but structured reflection and multiple perspectives make it a strength rather than a weakness.

items.stem: Examine the view that theories are of limited value in analysing small-scale, local engagement. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Theories are valuable at the local level if applied flexibly and tested against the evidence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: theories were designed for interstate relations (realism); local issues involve personalities and contingencies; risk of forcing evidence into theory. Arguments against: feminism, Marxism and constructivism apply at all levels; theory explains patterns beyond the case; concepts such as power and legitimacy are universal. Possible judgement: Theories are valuable at the local level if applied flexibly and tested against the evidence. items.stem: "A single detailed case study is more valuable than several brief examples in answering a stimulus question." Discuss.
items.answer: Depth is essential, but the strongest answers combine detailed cases with explicit comparison.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: depth allows analysis of actors and causes; specific evidence; avoids superficial lists. Arguments against: comparison needs at least two cases; range shows breadth of understanding; one case may be unrepresentative. Supported judgement: Depth is essential, but the strongest answers combine detailed cases with explicit comparison. items.stem: Discuss the importance of evidence selection and reflection in producing a convincing analysis of a political issue. [15]
items.answer: Convincing analysis depends on well-selected evidence and honest reflection on its limits.
